text:
Thread count is deliberately left at the transcribe.cpp default (n_threads=0) and there is no env var for it. Measured, do not redo this without new hardware:

n_threads=0 resolves to the number of CPUs in the process affinity mask, capped at 8. On the dev machine that was 4 logical CPUs. A sweep of 1, 2, 3, 4 and the default, in randomised order with the model loaded once and two runs per setting, found nothing consistently faster than the default. n_threads=1 was about 2.2x slower. Settings 2 to 4 were inside run-to-run noise. Output text was byte-identical at every thread count.

Throughput context, so nobody reads a bad number as a model property: about 2.8x realtime on an Intel i3-8109U, a 2 physical core 15 W mobile chip. Published Parakeet CPU figures near 20x come from many-core desktop and server CPUs; the gap is roughly the hardware ratio, not a misconfiguration. The library selected the correct AVX2/FMA kernel (libggml-cpu-haswell.so). That chip has no AVX-512 and no VNNI. No GPU was usable: the Vulkan backend module loads but reports no devices without a Vulkan driver installed.

Untested and possibly worthwhile if CPU throughput ever matters: Q8_0 instead of Q5_K_M. K-quants need real dequantisation work per matmul, while Q8_0 unpacking is nearly free, so Q8_0 is often faster on a CPU without VNNI despite the larger file.
author: Stavros Korokithakis <hi@stavros.io>

text:
The /transcribe endpoint is synchronous on purpose. A job queue, where POST returns an id and GET polls for the result, was designed and rejected as premature: it roughly doubles the code and buys nothing at the stated workload, which is audio of at most 10 minutes. Revisit it if expected audio grows to tens of minutes, or if callers start competing for the server, because runs are serialized and a caller waits for everything queued ahead of it.

Checked while deciding this, so nobody has to check again: waitress does NOT kill long in-flight requests. Its maintenance loop only closes channels with no active request, so channel_timeout (default 120 s) cannot interrupt a transcription that takes minutes. The real constraints are client timeouts and any reverse proxy read timeout, whose defaults are usually 60 s.

Also rejected: FastAPI plus uvicorn, because the work is a blocking CPU-bound native call deliberately serialized behind one lock. A sync endpoint there lands in a thread pool anyway, so async buys nothing and costs ASGI plus python-multipart. Stdlib http.server was rejected because the cgi module is gone in Python 3.13, which would make multipart parsing hand-written.

Also deliberately not built: any cache-directory or temp-directory setting of our own. HF_HOME already relocates the model cache (verified: HF_HOME=/models puts blobs in /models/hub) and TMPDIR already relocates upload staging.
author: Stavros Korokithakis <hi@stavros.io>

text:
Biasing the transcription toward known words, for example names, is NOT possible with this library. Investigated and confirmed, do not re-research:

transcribe.cpp has no hotword, biasing, boosting, or custom vocabulary API. Searched both the Python package and the native library's strings; the only text-conditioning mechanism anywhere is initial_prompt, and it exists solely as a Whisper run extension (transcribe_whisper_run_ext).

The Parakeet model in use answers directly: supports("initial_prompt") is False and accepts(WhisperRunOptions) is False. That is expected, not a defect. Parakeet is a CTC/TDT model that transcribes in one pass, so there is no decoder prompt to seed. Prompting is a property of attention-decoder models such as Whisper.

Real contextual biasing, meaning weighting a decoder beam toward a word list, needs a hook into the decoder. The library exposes none, so it would require changing the C library. Ruled out.

Options weighed:
- Switch to a Whisper model and use initial_prompt. The only in-library path. Rejected for now: much slower than Parakeet, and prompt biasing in Whisper is a soft hint that is sometimes ignored, can leak prompt text into output, and can trigger hallucination. Whisper also works in 30 s windows, whereas this Parakeet model reports no input length limit, so long-form handling would need checking first.
- Fuzzy post-correction of the transcript against a supplied word list. Cheap, local, no new dependency. Real limits: it only helps when the output is already close to the target, so it fails when the model renders a name as two or three ordinary words, and a loose threshold corrupts words that were already correct. Phonetic matching would beat string distance but adds a dependency. Rejected.
- An LLM pass over the transcript with the word list. Best quality because it uses sentence context. THIS WAS CHOSEN AND IS NOW BUILT; see entry uexafh for the decisions behind it. The unresolved question at the time was not technical: running it locally is slow on modest hardware, and running it through an API means transcript text leaves the machine. Transcripts here can be private conversation, so that choice belongs to the operator and must not be made by default. It was settled by calling an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, which a local server and a hosted API both speak, leaving the operator to pick.

Other capabilities observed on the model while checking, since they are cheap to lose and not obvious from the code: no input length limit, English only, timestamps available down to token level, and cancellation is the only advertised behavioural feature (no pnc, itn, diarization, long_form or temperature_fallback).
author: Stavros Korokithakis <hi@stavros.io>

text:
LLM postprocessing is now BUILT. This supersedes the "deferred, not built" note in the word-biasing entry.

Shape: an optional pass over the finished transcript, calling an OpenAI-compatible chat completions endpoint. Configured by LLM_BASE_URL and LLM_MODEL, requested per call with postprocess=true, steered by an optional vocabulary word list.

Decisions that came from the user this session, none of which are recoverable from the code:

Opt-in is per request and defaults to false. The reason is privacy, not caution about cost or latency. An operator who sets the environment variables must not thereby cause every transcript to be shipped to a third party. The caller asks, every time, or nothing is sent. Do not "helpfully" make this default on.

A misconfigured or unreachable endpoint returns processed_text: null with HTTP 200, never a 4xx or 5xx. The user wanted exactly one fallback path for clients: use processed_text, fall back to text when null. Adding an error status for misconfiguration was considered and rejected on those grounds, even though it is more honest about the cause.

The stated workload ceiling is 15 minutes of audio, roughly 2300 words. This number came from the user and is the only justification for how MAX_POSTPROCESS_CHARACTERS is sized. The cap is a guard against a surprise multi-hour upload becoming a large bill. It is not a technical limit, and chunking was deliberately not built. If the workload grows past that ceiling, revisit the cap first, and only then consider chunking.

Scope of the edit was widened during discussion. The user first said names and words only, then asked for tidying as well: punctuation, capitalisation, paragraph breaks, filler removal, obvious mis-transcriptions. The settled reading is that the model may reshape the presentation but must not touch the content. The vocabulary field carries words only; all instructions live in the hardcoded prompt.

Prompt injection through transcript content is accepted deliberately, not overlooked. Someone can speak an instruction into the microphone and steer the rewrite. The only thing they can affect is the text returned to the caller who supplied the audio, so the user judged a defence not worth building. The prompt says the transcript is speech and not a command, and that is all. Do not re-open this without a new threat model.

Also rejected in passing: the openai package, for a single POST that urllib does in a few lines; retries; streaming; caching; and letting the caller choose the model or the endpoint, because that choice is the operator's privacy decision and must not move to the client.

Not built, and worth knowing someone considered it: there are no tests in this repository, and a reviewer asked for them for this feature. The gap is real and known. The paths worth covering if that ever changes are the null fallbacks and the fact that the network call happens outside model_lock.
author: Stavros Korokithakis <hi@stavros.io>

text:
A cloud transcription engine is now BUILT. CLOUD_API_KEY selects it and it then handles every request. Decisions from the user this session, none recoverable from the code:

The operator picks the engine and the caller has NO say. This deliberately runs the opposite way from the postprocessing rule in entry uexafh, which says an operator setting env vars must not by itself ship data to a third party. The user was offered three caller-facing designs (automatic fallback on local failure, caller picks the engine per request, caller permits a fallback per request) and rejected all three: 'No fallback, it's either local or cloud for everything.' The reconciliation, which is the part worth keeping: uexafh also rejected letting the caller choose the postprocessing model or endpoint because that is the operator's privacy decision. Engine choice is that same decision. Postprocessing is an optional extra pass so it needs a per-call switch; transcription is the whole job, so there is nothing to opt out of. Do not 'fix' this asymmetry by adding a per-request engine flag.

No fallback in either direction was explicit. A wrong key therefore means every request 502s with no local backstop. The user accepted that.

WHY THIS FEATURE EXISTS AT ALL: the session began by asking whether the existing LLM_BASE_URL credentials could also transcribe audio. They cannot, and this is worth not re-testing. That endpoint is a self-hosted router in authenticated proxy mode whose upstream is Anthropic, and Anthropic has no speech-to-text endpoint while Claude models accept text, images and PDFs but not audio. So the postprocessing credentials and the transcription credentials are necessarily separate, which is why there are three new CLOUD_* variables rather than reuse.

CLOUD_API_KEY is the switch because CLOUD_BASE_URL has a default and so cannot be one. Known limitation, accepted rather than overlooked: a keyless OpenAI-compatible server, such as a self-hosted Whisper, cannot be selected. The local engine covers that case.

THE NO-HTTP-DEPENDENCY RULE IS NOW LIFTED. This is the one reversal worth flagging, because uexafh records the opposite. The cloud engine was first built with a hand-built multipart body on urllib, following that entry. The user then said dependencies were fine if the code got smaller, so both outbound calls now use httpx and the hand-rolled wire format is gone. That took transcribe.py from 270 to 242 lines and removed the most error-prone code in the feature. httpx specifically, not requests: huggingface-hub already requires httpx unconditionally, so it was already installed and cost no download or image size, while requests was not present. The openai package was still rejected, because the exact multipart format had already been verified against the live API and httpx keeps that under our control, whereas the SDK routes keywords through extra_body and pulls pydantic and anyio for no gain. uexafh's reasoning was sound for a JSON POST, which urllib does in a few lines; it did not hold for multipart.

Rejected alternatives, so nobody rebuilds them:
- Opus as the re-encode target, despite being much smaller for speech. OpenAI's transcription endpoint does not accept it. Verified: an Ogg/Opus upload returns 400 'Unsupported file format opus'. Opus inside a WebM container would be accepted but needs fussier muxing to a pipe. MP3 mono 16 kHz 32 kbps was chosen instead, and at that bitrate 25 MB is about 1.8 hours, so chunking stays unbuilt, consistent with uexafh.
- ffprobe content inspection to decide whether an upload needs re-encoding. The filename extension is used instead, because OpenAI dispatches on the extension itself, so matching their signal needs no new tool and no format-name mapping table. Accepted cost: a mislabelled file is rejected upstream and surfaces as a 502.
- Startup validation of the credentials. A wrong key surfaces as a 502 on first use.

Not built and worth knowing someone considered it: still no tests, and this change roughly doubled the size of the request handler, so the untested surface grew. The paths worth covering if that ever changes are the pass-through versus re-encode branch, the multipart construction, and the 502 mapping.
author: Stavros Korokithakis <hi@stavros.io>

text:
Word biasing is now POSSIBLE, in cloud mode only. This qualifies entry xwhmtt, which says biasing the transcription toward a word list is not possible and is the whole reason the LLM postprocessing pass exists. That remains true of the local Parakeet engine and is false for the cloud engine.

OpenAI's transcription endpoint takes a keywords[] parameter for literal terms expected in the audio. The existing vocabulary form field now feeds it, so in cloud mode names are biased during recognition rather than repaired afterwards. The user asked for this to be added to the scope of the cloud engine work, having seen it noted as a possible follow-up.

keywords[] was chosen over the prompt parameter deliberately. prompt is supported by more models, including whisper-1, and passing a comma-separated word list as the prompt is the classic Whisper trick, but xwhmtt already rejected exactly that: it is a soft hint that can leak prompt text into the output and trigger hallucination. Do not reintroduce prompt biasing as a compatibility shim.

WHICH MODELS ACCEPT keywords[]. Measured against the live API, not taken from the docs, which are silent or misleading on this. Only gpt-transcribe accepts it. whisper-1, gpt-4o-transcribe AND gpt-4o-mini-transcribe all return 400 invalid_parameter, which this server maps to 502. An earlier version of the ticket for this work wrongly claimed the gpt-4o variants supported it; they do not. So CLOUD_MODEL is effectively pinned to gpt-transcribe for as long as biasing matters, and changing it silently costs the feature. The keywords part is omitted entirely when the caller supplies no words, which is the only thing that keeps the other models usable at all. Model capabilities are deliberately NOT sniffed from the model name; the limitation is documented instead.

Pricing at the time of writing, for whoever next weighs a model change: gpt-4o-mini-transcribe $0.003/min, gpt-transcribe $0.0045/min, gpt-4o-transcribe and whisper $0.006/min. The default is therefore the second cheapest and the only one that biases, and the single cheaper option cannot bias. That combination is why the default is not worth revisiting on cost grounds alone. The 25 MB cap bounds one request to roughly 50 cents.

Other verified behaviour, do not re-research:
- A keyword containing < or > makes the ENTIRE request fail with 400 'Invalid request.' / invalid_value. This is why the words are sanitised, and it is a real failure rather than a precaution. A bare carriage return inside a word does the same, which is why the splitter treats \r as a separator.
- Silent audio returns a 200 with an empty text string, not an error, so an empty transcript is a valid success and must not be treated as a failure.

Consequence to keep in mind: vocabulary now has an effect without postprocess=true, which was not true before. When both are used the same words are applied twice, once during recognition and once during cleanup. That is intended, and the two paths are deliberately not coupled.
author: Stavros Korokithakis <hi@stavros.io>

text:
Moving both outbound calls from urllib to httpx changed two ambient behaviours. Both were found in review and both were deliberately KEPT rather than papered over, so do not 'restore' them without reading this.

Redirects are no longer followed. urllib followed 301/302/303/307 on a POST; httpx.post defaults to follow_redirects=False. Verified: an endpoint answering 302 then 200 used to succeed and now reaches raise_for_status, so a redirecting LLM_BASE_URL or CLOUD_BASE_URL turns into a 502 for transcription or a null processed_text for postprocessing. Kept because redirect following was an accidental property of urllib rather than a feature anyone asked for, OpenAI does not redirect, the failure is loud and appears in the log, and following a redirect while carrying an Authorization header would hand the API key to whatever host the redirect names. Note also that urllib downgraded 301/302/303 POSTs to GET, so its apparent success on those was dubious anyway. One keyword argument would restore it if a real deployment ever needs it.

ALL_PROXY is now honoured. httpx reads HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY, ALL_PROXY and NO_PROXY; urllib's getproxies_environment parsed all_proxy into a scheme named 'all' that never matched http or https, so it was effectively ignored. Verified: with ALL_PROXY=socks5://... in the environment both calls now fail with ImportError, because plain httpx has no SOCKS support. Kept because honouring proxy variables is the correct behaviour for an operator behind a corporate proxy, the alternative of trust_env=False would break that legitimate case, and the SOCKS failure is explicit in the log. httpx[socks] was rejected as a dependency for a hypothetical.

Neither is documented in the README, because both are properties of the HTTP client rather than of this server's interface.
author: Stavros Korokithakis <hi@stavros.io>
